title: History and Place Names
summary: A guide to Long Island place names, variant spellings, cross-references, uncertain locations, and names that William Wallace Tooker questioned or interpreted cautiously.
content:
Introduction

Long Island placenames preserve layered histories: Indigenous words and personal names, English and Dutch spellings, colonial deed language, later map labels, and modern town names. William Wallace Tooker's 1911 dictionary remains an important doorway into that record because it gathers many early forms in one place.

The history explains how placenames can be read across references when they do not fit neatly as individual map sites.

Variant Spellings and Cross-References

Colonial writers wrote Indigenous names phonetically, and spelling could change from one document to another. Tooker's dictionary therefore includes many short entries that simply point to another form. These spellings generally belong with the fuller placename record.

  • Wimbaccoe is represented with Winippague at Bergen Island.
  • Wingatthappagh is represented with Winganhauppauge at Champlain's Creek in Islip.
  • Wynycomic is represented with Winnecomac at Commack.
  • Waracto is represented with Warratta.
  • Wiandance is represented with Wyandance / Wyandanch.

Names Not Mapped as Separate Sites

Some names are preserved as research context rather than as individual map markers. This happens when a record is only a spelling variant, when the exact location is not identified in the available source, or when Tooker questioned whether the name was Indigenous in origin.

Names Tooker Questioned

Tooker questioned whether several names were Indigenous in origin. These entries are useful because they show how he corrected local traditions as well as how uncertain names circulated.

  • Winket / Winkle Point: described as a corruption of English winkle, not an Indigenous placename.
  • Wainscott: treated by Tooker as not Aboriginal despite earlier explanations.
  • Bassalona / Barcelona: connected with a possible non-Indigenous Barcelona tradition.
  • Bostwicks: associated with a later personal name on Gardiner's Island.
  • Chocomount: described as not Indigenous, or at most a highly corrupted form.
  • Cobb, Costeyick, Ebwons, Genissee, Goorgo, Ligonee, Lusam, and Oquenock: entries where Tooker or later comparison points away from a secure Indigenous placename.

Places Beyond the Current Map Area

Some Tooker entries lie outside the current Long Island map area but are included here for context because they appear in the same regional record.

  • Aquehonga Manacknong and Eghquaons: Staten Island entries.
  • Pagganck: Governor's Island, formerly Nut Island.
  • Cockenoe Island: an island off Westport, Connecticut, connected with a person important in Long Island records.
  • Sawgogue: a Rhode Island locality.
  • Shattemuc, Nechtank, and related entries: Manhattan or Hudson/East River contexts.

Places Requiring Further source context

A few entries identify a general area but not enough detail for a public map marker. These remain useful research leads.

  • Castateum: a salt-meadow tract called the westermost flat, without a secure modern point.
  • Wooruskhouse: a place in Rev. Azariah Horton's journal, described as three miles from West Neck, but without a direction.
  • Wallace / Wallage: conflicting Woodbury and Westbury associations.
  • Tersarge: location and etymology remain uncertain in the available source record.
  • Tinnie's Water Hole: a sensitive place story where the exact water-hole location should be handled carefully.

How Map Markers Are Used

Blue markers on placename records show broad modern reference points: a town center, waterbody, creek, bay, neck, point, island, or other identifiable feature. They do not claim to mark exact historical boundaries. Green markers are reserved for more specific locations supported by the source record.

Sources

The main source for the placename import is William Wallace Tooker's Indian Place-Names on Long Island and Islands Adjacent. The placename work also compares Tooker's entries with John A. Strong's historical work, town records, patents, maps, and related local histories where those sources are available.
